title: Choosing a text type

match.reason: The bank points cover text structure, language and text purposes, but none teaches choosing a text form such as a letter, report, speech or story to fit its purpose and audience, so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Choosing a text type
card: A text type is the form a piece of writing takes, such as a letter, a report, a speech or a story. Each form has its own features and suits certain jobs.
Start with your purpose: why are you writing? You might want to inform, persuade, entertain or explain. Then think about your audience: who will read or hear it?
A speech is spoken aloud to a live audience, so it uses direct address and a strong, clear voice. A report gives facts in an organised, formal way. A story entertains with characters and events.
A letter is written to a particular person or group. Its tone can be formal or friendly, depending on who reads it and why you are writing.
draft.remember: Choose the form that fits your purpose and your audience.

a.q: Zara wants to tell her whole school why they should recycle more, and she will present it at assembly. Which text type suits this best?
opts: A persuasive speech
A recount of her week
A scientific report
A fairy tale
a.why: Her purpose is to persuade, and the audience will hear her live at assembly. A speech is made for that job. A fairy tale entertains, so it does not suit the purpose.
a.clue: Think about both why she is writing and how the audience will receive it.

b.q: Mr Ito wants to give the Year 7 parents in his class clear facts about next term's camp: dates, costs and what to pack. Which text type suits this best?
opts: A formal letter with the details set out clearly
A short story about a camp that goes wrong
A speech with strong emotional language
A poem about the joy of camping
b.why: His purpose is to inform, and the audience is parents who need clear facts. A formal letter sent to them can do this directly. A story can also be about camp, but it entertains and does not give the facts parents need.
b.clue: Match the form to the purpose of giving facts, not to the topic of camp.

b.best: A formal letter with the details set out clearly

problems.detail: The right option is the only one that echoes the stem ('details set out clearly' matches 'clear facts'), so a student could pick it without knowing which form suits informing.
'the Year 7 parents in his class' is awkward: the parents are not in his class. Better: 'the parents of the Year 7 students in his class'.

a.q: Zara wants to convince her whole school to recycle more, and she will present her ideas at assembly. Which text type suits this best?
opts: A persuasive speech
A story about a lost bottle
A formal report of facts
A friendly letter to a friend
a.why: Her purpose is to persuade, and the audience will hear her live at assembly. A speech is made for that job. A report gives facts in a formal way, but it is not built to be spoken aloud to win over a crowd.
a.clue: Think about both why she is writing and how the audience will receive it.

b.q: Mr Ito wants to tell the parents of the Year 7 students in his class about next term's camp: dates, costs and what to pack. Which text type suits this best?
opts: A letter sent home to each family
A short story about a camp trip
A speech to the Year 7 students
A poem about life in the bush
b.why: His purpose is to inform, and his audience is the parents. A letter is written to a particular group, so it reaches them directly. A speech to the students goes to the wrong audience, and a story or poem entertains rather than informs.
b.clue: Check two things: who needs the details, and what job the text must do.
